prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms are interrogated in a magic-wavelength lattice, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 regime

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B022 alone, Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements I find that nobody argues against the science, and the support comes from members with different criteria (instrument, tests of fundamental physics, geodesy). The chair asks whether the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice is a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion prizes. I think it is, and the distinction can be stated in measurable terms. Single-ion clocks get their accuracy from one trapped particle and are limited by signal-to-noise and averaging time. The lattice, by choosing the wavelength at which the two clock levels shift equally, lets thousands of atoms be held Doppler- and recoil-free without a first-order light shift. That changes statistics and systematics together, and it is what made 1e-18 comparisons, millimetre-scale redshift measurements and clock-to-clock links over fibre routine. The comb is the ruler that reads out the optical frequency; the lattice is a different kind of oscillator reference. On credit, my reading is that Katori carries the concept and the first strontium lattice demonstration, and Ye's group carried it to the accuracy and stability frontier, including the many-body and density-shift work. That is a defensible two-name split. I do not need the redefinition of the second to have happened: the scientific case rests on reproduced measurements, and the committee should not tie recognition to a metrology decision.
statement.case_against: I keep the same objections, and round 1 has made me put a little more weight on them. First, the 2005 and 2012 prizes are adjacent ground, so the citation must name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime and must not say 'atomic clocks' or 'frequency metrology'. Second, the credit is clean in structure but not complete: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov and the NIST and PTB groups made essential contributions and cannot be named. Lindroth and Olsson are right that I was too quick to say Takamoto is covered by Katori; he is a co-worker in Katori's group, which is why I still think he fits under that name, but I have not checked the authorship and priority record and would want that done. Third, Mehlig's objection that the underlying physics is an application of known atomic physics is not empty. It is a real difference of taste between a measurement advance and a new organising idea, and I do not claim it is settled.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B045 because a bulk topological invariant is a new organising idea, and regards the lattice clock as an application of known atomic physics (magic-wavelength trapping, Lamb-Dicke confinement) that overlaps the 2005 and 2012 prizes. He still names B022 as the safer prize if uncontested credit is weighted above field-level influence.
responses.response: I accept that the ingredients were known: light shifts and Lamb-Dicke confinement are textbook. What was not known, and was contested by good people at the time, is that a many-atom ensemble could be held at a magic wavelength with the residual shifts small enough to reach 1e-18 and reproduced by several laboratories. That is an experimental result about what nature allows, and it was not obvious in advance. I agree that an invariant that classifies matter is a deeper idea, but for B045 the committee itself cannot settle the trio: Olsson wants Hasan and drops Mele, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang is outside every proposal. You describe B022 as the safer prize; in a final vote I would weigh that, because a prize with a disputed credit set is exposed in a way a prize with two clear names is not. I would not move B045 above B022 unless the documentation shows the 2D quantum spin Hall unit is separable from the 3D story.

responses.point: Olsson supports B022 with Katori and Ye, but says the early strontium lattice priority (Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde) can only partly be settled from memory and that two names cannot represent everyone. She also proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for B045, not Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
responses.response: I agree that priority has to be documented and I do not want to rely on my memory. The test I would apply to the early papers is simple: who first proposed the magic wavelength with a numerical estimate, who first demonstrated it with a narrow clock transition in a lattice, and who first showed that the uncertainty could be driven to the 1e-17 and 1e-18 range with agreement between laboratories. As I remember the record, those three steps lead to Katori for the first two and to Ye's group for the third, with Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley as important contributors to the second and third. If the checks show the order differently, I would revisit the pair. Where I part from you is on B045: dropping Mele to credit Hasan removes half of the Z2 theory in exchange for an observation, and I see no reading that fixes the credit problem for that part. This is another reason I keep B022 ahead of it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp and argues that the 2016 prize covered a different discovery. He also says the credit is the main weakness and names B022 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I think your reasoning about 2016 is sound, since defects and phase transitions in 2D matter are not the same as a Z2 invariant protected by time-reversal symmetry. Your own list of weaknesses is where I would be most careful: the unit may look arbitrary against the 3D story, the BHZ proposal and Zhang are outside the names, and the Kane-Mele phase is not realised in graphene. That is a lot of caveats for one prize part, and you say yourself that you would sooner see B022 awarded cleanly than force a contested trio. I take that seriously as a statement of preference. I keep B045 as my first alternative if the committee wants a condensed-matter prize, with the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and its HgTe observation as the unit, and not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B022 and wants the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice, not clocks in general, while noting that credit is not complete (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom).
responses.response: We agree on the wording, and I have written my citation so that the lattice and the 1e-18 regime are in the text and the comb and single-ion work are not claimed. I also accept your correction on credit. The honest statement is that Katori's priority on the concept and Ye's on performance are what I am sure of, while the remaining groups made necessary contributions that a two-name prize cannot reflect. I would not describe the credit as 'cleanest' without that qualification. Where I would still disagree is on discount: the incompleteness is the usual kind for experimental physics with a handful of leading groups, and it is smaller than for B002, B046 or B039.

uncertainties: Exact priority among Katori, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Lemonde for the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstrations is from memory and should be checked against the primary papers before the final vote.

Whether other members accept the lattice as an invention distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion prizes. My answer is yes, but it rests on a judgement about the physics that Mehlig and Danielsson do not share.
Whether the committee treats a measurement advance that has so far produced bounds, not detections, as a discovery in the sense of the will.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would be wise. I think not, but I cannot rule out that some members see it as the natural date.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1 and noted to the chair. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during my PhD; Hall (2005 laureate) worked closely with the JILA environment in which Jun Ye is active. My profile records no co-authorship or collaboration with Ye or Katori. I lead quantum sensing in WACQT, which is based at Chalmers (shared with Johansson), and I am involved in a slow-light filter company, which gives me an interest in precision measurement as such but no financial or institutional tie to any B022 candidate. I do not think this requires recusal, but I would accept the chair's decision. I have no specific tie to the credited names of B045 or B033.
